inlines.text: Opening thought
Hello🙂! If you’re reading this, you must either be a leader from the church that congregates at Lavender, or from the
Thoughts on the Bible
document, or one of my close friends.

I wanted to write in detail about what I am convinced that God has led me to! I hope that as you read it, you’ll read it in the best possible light, meaning to say, I hope you’ll read every word as it was written with utmost love in the hope of unity ultimately aiming to bring glory to our Lord and Saviour, Jesus, our precious Son of God.

As of this writing (2/10/2024), I think there are 2 major thoughts that I want to express, with love! The first being why I feel convicted to explore beyond LCOC, and the second is my thoughts on the theology of baptism. I don’t think this document will express the entirety of my thoughts perfectly, but I think it’s a good place to start if you want to understand where I’m coming from!
In His love,
Alp
Why I feel convicted to explore beyond LCOC

I’ll share what I wrote in my journal that I shared with a close group of friends on Telegram on the 24th of September. Have added and edited some stuff for more clarity! Before reading it, do know that:
“Everything I do, I do it for the sake of Christ! That godly love will abound with godly wisdom and godly humility.” - alp, 2024
Note: There are some words that may be more easily taken offense at, I’ve added footnotes like [this

] that can be found at the bottom of the document for clarity on what I precisely meant! All in love❤️, without arrogance or wanting to belittle efforts done for the sake of Christ! I’ve also chosen to replace some words by italicising them because I’ve since seen a new POV and wish to express it differently.
My conviction
I think the Lord has convicted me that it's finally time to
explore what’s out there
. I have
attempted to be
vocal about my position regarding doctrinal stances during LCOC's leadership meeting, that
I’ve taken a soft stance towards the understanding that baptism is for the remission of sins,
and that I see justification in the Sola Fide’s pov that we are justified through faith in Christ, and genuine faith leads to
all the things that Scripture has stressed on:
belief, repentance, confession, and baptism. This has led to the
cautious stopping

of my service (teaching the 'visitors' class, Philen and Chloe; potentially JELLY event). But I speak all these with love and nuances, for it is wise and fair for a church to exert church discipline and restrict teaching roles if they feel that the teacher may represent unsound Scriptural teachings correctly. Ultimately the thing that convicted me was these things happening at the same time:

In my view, I sensed a lack of urgency and recognition of how spiritually dead we are without Christ. This shows up in our sermons and Bible classes, where there's not enough emphasis on our desperate need for Jesus’ redemption in every area of life. I do acknowledge that some people see this to a certain extent and genuinely want to help those who struggle with this at LCOC. I, too, would like to contribute where I can, so the church can be uplifted, and we can all grasp our deep need for Jesus in every aspect of life. It’s a challenging task, but one I believe is worth pursuing.

However, this effort will only thrive if the church and its leaders remain receptive. If this message becomes a burden or a "thorn in the flesh" to the leadership, I fear it may do more harm than good. I don’t want to work against the leadership or cause further division. I felt this spirit hit its limit when my concerns seemed to boil down to, “Ok, I hear you… but wrong doctrine.” That response missed the heart of what I was trying to convey. It felt as though people were content with a shallow view of the gospel and didn’t desire to see it in its fullness.

When we approach Scripture in Bible study, it often feels like the focus shifts to defending a particular doctrine rather than simply understanding and appreciating the message the text is trying to convey. There's also a sense of needing to keep things under wraps, as though the Bible can't speak for itself and that if people read it on their own, they might come to the wrong conclusions.

Lastly, I've come to realize my own inadequacy in teaching the kind of gospel truth that truly inspires people to give their lives for our God, King, and Servant, Jesus. As someone who hasn’t been fed, I recognize that I’m not in the position to be feeding others. Continuing like this feels dangerous, as it could easily lead to spiritual coldness, where you just do the bare minimum. Of course, there are nuances to this, but ultimately the question is: "Is your faith stumbling?" If it is, then something needs to be done.

Ultimately, my decision is not driven by a desire to align with a "correct" doctrine but by the realization that I want my faith to grow in an environment where we confront the sinfulness in our lives and let the Word convict our hearts. This means I’m not concerned

with whether the Church of Christ’s perspective or the reformist’s perspective is right—I see the validity in both. What I seek is a church that prioritizes what truly matters in my opinion: a life fully transformed by Christ, rather than a focus on doctrinal precision that divides God’s people.

I understand that I could remain at LCOC without serving in any teaching roles, and I would be okay with that. However, I believe it’s wiser for me to seek guidance from leaders who not only love the Lord deeply but also understand my perspective. I want to be led by those who demonstrate a level of spiritual maturity I can wholeheartedly respect and submit to in humility, rather than wrestle with feelings of disconnection or frustration.

I want to love my Lord and my God with all my heart, soul, mind, and strength, and I think that God has used my life here at LCOC for a purpose, but that purpose has perhaps since been fulfilled. I eagerly await what God has in waiting for me! Yet, I won't
start exploring
till Dec onwards, if I am still allowed to serve for the remaining events I've committed for, JELLY and Youth Camp, for I would want to fulfil what I had committed to.
God is good! Jesus is Lord! ❤️
P.S
Please don't read this and think that
I’m against the church leaders!

Most have been kind, patient, and wanting to understand where I'm coming from. I see genuine humility in Uncle Ivan, I see sacrifices and tact made by Uncle Patrick and Joel in reaching out to me and relaying the leader's judgement on my responsibilities, I see Uncle Peter's heart in recognising that the current state of things is far too short, and he has the desire to improve for our sake, Uncle Tat Chuen trying super hard to understand where I'm coming from, Prakash for his love in wanting to show me the truth, Uncle Boon Quang for always looking out for my financial well-being in every event, making sure that I can attend all church-events freely, Uncle Stephen for supporting me financially and for his zeal for continuing the gospel work in Cambodia.
P.P.S

All of you who are in here are my beloved valuable brothers and sisters in Christ in different areas of my lives! Please read this and handle your thoughts with tremendous love and care so as to not stumble others! I'm ok with y'all talking about it with others, but I trust that you'll exercise plenty of discernment. May God be glorified in your action!
P.P.P.S
I'll still be going to LCOC till God convicts me of what is best.
Having this level of conviction
is new to me and I'm still pondering on how I can best serve my friends at LCOC and my family at NECOC till then.
P.P.P.P.S
Upon typing all the encouragement I've seen, my heart has wavered a bit. I pray that from now till Dec, God will convict me of what He wants me to do.
Not as I will, but as He wills. To Christ be all!
P^5.S
I hope that all this P.Ss gives a glimpse into my heart, character, and intention beyond mere lifeless words.

Though I fall short, by God’s grace and through His infinite love being poured out into me, I too am willingly compelled to love my fellow “beggars of grace”. So, if you have any questions or clarifications on what I meant, please feel free to reach out to me! I would want to listen and understand!
Thoughts down the line
Some friends asked me why did I leave and I typed out some response, have shared it below for record keeping and journaling of my faith journey.
11 March 2025
Turkey friend [10-Mar-25 11:54 PM]
So alp if baptism was not an issue for you, why did you leave lcoc? I forgot why you left HAHA i thought it was baptism!
Alphaeus, [11-Mar-25 12:17 AM]
i left cos they "softly excommunicated" me and I felt that me staying would lead to more friction rather than building each other up in love!

At that point, I was even ok to preach that baptism was for the remission of sins and a "necessary" ordinance to enter into God's church (because even lutherans and presbyterians have a high view of baptism).

My main issue was the broader theme of hermeneutic and the lack of Christocentric teachings. But those were issues I wanted to stay and help address, provided the church was willing and we could partner on it!

But alas, it was not this season of time as by God's providence, the leadership and I were not able to communicate and understand each other's POV + the fear of false doctrine coming from me didn't help as well.

So at one Saturday Men's meeting, they decided that enough was enough and removed me from my leadership role, thus "softly excommunicating" me, but they were open to me coming back to listen. But I foresaw that my presence and interaction with the youth there would naturally always cause suspicion because they would never know what I was teaching, even in an informal setting.
And so, regrettably, unfortunately, with full sadness, I left LCOC.
Theology of Baptism

To re-emphasise, my main qualm with why I feel convicted to explore beyond LCOC is not due to the COC’s understanding of baptism. As of this writing (7/10/2024), I would gladly choose to submit to our understanding, that baptism is truly for the remission of sins (Matt 26:28, Mark 1:4, Luke 3:3, Acts 2:38) and the ordained act by which God justifies and washes away our sins. But I also believe there must be detailed nuances in understanding the Sola Fide’s POV and seeing that they’re also genuine Christians who love Jesus and also strive to be biblically-based. This means that when you read my thoughts on the verses below, it’s not meant to debate or argue what baptism truly constitutes, for my understanding is:
Whoever wants to follow Jesus will naturally seek to be baptised

(whether it be for the remission of sins, or for the outward proclamation of an inward faith)! Baptism in action or idea is an essential aspect of being a follower of Jesus. Whether in its symbolism of an inward faith or the obedience to the ritualistic ordained act that grants salvation.

The thoughts are meant to show that I am aware of COC’s understanding of all the verses used to support the essential nature of baptism for the remission of sins. But I also think there is an equally coherent justification for Sola Fide’s POV. I understand that it’s impossible to cover all the details, nor do I have the capability or time to do so, but whatever is there, is my best attempt to present my current thoughts on it with the time I have (while balancing daily work, daily fellowship w the saints, daily Masters, biweekly careteam prep, biweekly sermon prep!). So do bear with what I have and help me by reading in the best-est of light!

Overall, after understanding the reformer’s doctrinal POV, the thing that helped me to see them as fellow brothers and sisters in Christ was how they handled Bible Study (every study led to revealing a truth that pointed me to my need for Jesus!), and their lives (they were very intentional in growing and speaking of God in all areas of their life. In meetups and outside activity, it always pointed to God).
A little dive into tangilizing the “why” and “how” we understand the Bible

26/1/26: Before diving into the bible verses for baptism, I think it might be helpful to quickly understand helpful principles to understand Scripture + understand the background that kickstarted the reformation and restoration movement!

Every single word in the Bible was written for a specific purpose to illustrate God’s thoughts wrapped in different literary forms. The presence or even the absence of words are clues that reveal the author’s main intent. Additionally, we must also read the words with the lens from “their town”, for if we read it with “our town”’s lenses, we will not get the full picture and possibly misinterpret the original meaning.
26/1/26: After reading some sources (
Reviving the Ancient Faith: The Story of Churches of Christ in America by Richard T. Hughes
and
Churches of Christ history
) on the history of the restoration movement (the movement that ‘started’

the COC heritage), I’ve come to understand a bit more about the “whys” and “how” of the influences affecting COC thinking. So before going into the next section covering the verses regarding Baptism, it might be helpful to see the climate that birthed both perspectives. In as concisely as possible (you’ll probably have to google some of the terms to grasp the full weight of each word):

Restoration climate: Started in the 1800s. There was an explosion of denominational Christians everywhere. Lots of debates against each other, dividing believers. With an ecumenical + frontier spirit, Barton W. Stone and the Campbells wanted to unite Christendom by restoring the New Testament church on the commonest denominator, giving rise to the blueprint methodology of reading Scripture. The path forward they chose was to reject man's tradition and return solely to the authority of the Bible. Summed up with the famous slogan, “No Creed but the Bible, no name but Christian”.

Reformer climate: Started in the 1500s. There was a powerful, monolithic Catholic Church that had dominated Western Europe for centuries, with accumulated traditions, hierarchical authority, indulgences, and practices that many saw as drifting away from what’s biblical. Lots of internal corruption, political entanglement, and growing calls for change. With a reforming spirit, Martin Luther and later reformers like John Calvin and Ulrich Zwingli saw that the most helpful way to understand Scripture was through the five solas, giving rise to a return to apostolic Christianity. The path forward they chose was to reject human traditions and papal decrees that lacked clear biblical warrant and return solely to the authority of the Bible. Summed up with the famous slogans, “Sola Scriptura” (Scripture Alone), along with Sola Fide, Sola Gratia, Solus Christus, and Soli Deo Gloria.
Verses Emphasising Baptism
<26/1/26: for each verse and its explanation, perform a highlight/font color to signified which portion was emphasized on for coc or reform view>
1. Colossians 2:12
“Buried with Him in baptism, in which you also were raised with Him through faith in the working of God, who raised Him from the dead.”
COC Understanding
The Church of Christ emphasizes that
baptism is the means

by which believers participate in Christ's death, burial, and resurrection. They view this verse as linking baptism directly to the believer’s spiritual resurrection and thus see baptism as essential for receiving salvation and sharing in Christ's resurrection.
Sola Fide Understanding
Proponents of salvation through faith alone emphasize that the key phrase is "
through faith in the powerful working of God
." They argue that baptism is the outward symbol of an inward reality that has already occurred through faith. Baptism signifies this spiritual transformation, but
faith
is the means through which believers are spiritually raised with Christ, not the act of baptism itself.
Colossians 2:11-12 – Circumcision and Baptism
Colossians 2:11-12:

"In Him, you were also circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with Him in baptism, in which you were also raised with Him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised Him from the dead."
Paul is drawing a
symbolic parallel
between the
Old Covenant ritual of circumcision
and the
New Covenant practice of baptism
Additional Context
Main Idea of Colossians 2:

The chapter emphasizes Christ’s sufficiency for salvation and cautions against being led astray by human traditions or deceptive philosophies that detract from Him. Paul focuses on what God has accomplished through Christ's death, burial, and resurrection, and how believers participate in this through faith, which is symbolized by baptism. Baptism is presented as a sign of the believer’s spiritual burial and resurrection with Christ, but Paul underscores that it is faith in God's power that unites believers with Christ.
Cultural Clues:

In the 1st century, baptism was viewed as a profound act of identification with Christ’s death and resurrection. It was a significant public declaration, marking a person’s transition from their old life to new life in Christ. Paul’s language in this passage (especially verses 8–23) cautions against understanding baptism, or any other ritual, as inherently salvific. Instead, faith in Christ’s completed work is presented as central to salvation.
Circumcision
was the physical mark of the
Old Covenant
between God and His people, Israel, signifying that they were set apart as belonging to God. It was a
required physical sign
that a person (specifically, males) was part of God's covenant community.
Baptism
, in the New Covenant, is compared to circumcision. It is the
external sign
that someone is now united with Christ, having been "buried" with Him (symbolizing death to the old life) and "raised" with Him (symbolizing new life). But, as
Paul emphasizes
, this is a
spiritual transformation
—a "circumcision made without hands," meaning it’s not about physical rituals but about
faith
Theological Significance: Connecting Old and New Covenants
Circumcision of the Heart:
In the Old Testament, physical circumcision was an external sign of being part of God's people, but it was always meant to
point to a deeper reality
—the need for
circumcision of the heart
, a transformation on the inside, not just the outside. For instance, in
Deuteronomy 10:16
, God commands,
"Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn."
The prophets also echo this idea (e.g.,
Jeremiah 4:4
). Paul brings this concept to its
full realization in Christ
. In Colossians 2:11, he describes how Christ's work has spiritually "circumcised" believers, meaning they have put off the sinful nature and been given new life in Christ.
Baptism, then, is the same outward sign
of this inward transformation.
Abraham’s Faith Before Circumcision (Romans 4):
Paul reinforces this theological connection in
Romans 4
, where he explains how Abraham was justified by faith
before
he was circumcised. Abraham’s faith was counted as righteousness in
Genesis 15:6
, but circumcision was only instituted in
Genesis 17:10-11
. This shows that
faith, not circumcision
, was the true basis of Abraham’s righteousness before God. Paul makes this point explicitly in
Romans 4:9-12

“Is this blessedness only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? We have been saying that Abraham’s faith was credited to him as righteousness. Under what circumstances was it credited? Was it after he was circumcised, or before? It was not after, but before! And he received circumcision as a sign, a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. So then, he is the father of all who believe but have not been circumcised, in order that righteousness might be credited to them.”
Key Insight:
Circumcision was not the cause of Abraham’s righteousness, but a
sign and seal
of the faith he already had. Similarly, in the New Covenant,
baptism
is the
sign
of the new life a believer already has through faith, not the mechanism that causes the new life.
2. 1 Peter 3:21
“There is also an antitype which now saves us—baptism (not the removal of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God), through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.”
COC Understanding
: Baptism is directly linked to salvation in this verse, suggesting it plays a crucial role in the process of being saved.

The Church of Christ interprets this verse as a clear statement that baptism is part of the process of salvation. Peter’s comparison of baptism to the flood that saved Noah’s family suggests that baptism plays a key role in salvation, not just as a symbolic act, but as part of the believer’s response to God.
Sola Fide Understanding
: Peter clarifies that baptism saves not by the physical act itself, but by what it represents: a good conscience toward God, which comes through faith in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

Sola fide adherents point out that Peter clarifies that it is not the physical act of washing ("removal of the filth of the flesh") that saves, but rather the appeal of a good conscience toward God, which comes through faith in Christ’s resurrection. Baptism is seen as an outward expression of the inner reality of faith and the believer’s commitment to follow Christ.
Additional Context

This passage connects baptism to salvation by comparing it to the flood in Noah’s time. Peter clarifies that it is not the physical act of washing or the removal of dirt that saves but rather what it represents: a spiritual appeal to God for a good conscience, made possible through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The verse highlights that baptism is a symbol of salvation, with the focus being on faith in Christ’s resurrection as the basis for salvation.

You’re right to question where the focus on faith is in 1 Peter 3:21, as the text itself doesn’t explicitly mention “faith” in a direct manner. The emphasis is more on baptism as an act that represents an appeal to God for a good conscience, and the saving power is rooted in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Here’s why faith is sometimes inferred:

“Baptism… now saves you” – Peter is saying that baptism is tied to salvation, but he immediately clarifies not as a removal of dirt (i.e., not through the physical act itself) but as “an appeal to God for a good conscience”. The "appeal" or "pledge" to God for a good conscience is seen by many interpreters as implying an internal attitude of repentance and faith. In other words, the act of baptism is meaningful because it signifies a believer’s internal commitment or appeal to God, which in Christian theology, is connected with faith.

Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ – Peter ties the saving nature of baptism to Christ’s resurrection. Theologically, this means that baptism is effective not because of the act itself, but because it is connected to the power of Jesus’ resurrection, which Christians participate in through faith in Christ. Baptism symbolizes this participation in Christ's death and resurrection.

So, while faith is not mentioned explicitly, the appeal to God for a good conscience and the focus on the resurrection of Christ naturally lead to an understanding that faith in Christ’s work is behind the act of baptism. The act itself symbolizes an inner transformation that is associated with faith in the resurrection.
Cultural clues

: In Peter’s cultural context, water was often associated with cleansing, but Peter emphasizes that baptism is not just a physical act but a spiritual commitment. Baptism, like Noah's deliverance through water, is about faith in God's deliverance
3. Acts 2:38
Then Peter said to them, “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.”
COC Understanding (the “in order to / unto” view)
The Church of Christ sees this verse as one of the clearest statements that baptism is essential for the remission of sins. The Greek preposition
eis
here carries its most common meaning:
purpose, goal, or result
(“in order to obtain,” “unto,” or “for the purpose of”).
Peter links repentance and baptism together in one command, then attaches the purpose clause
eis aphesin hamartion
(“for the remission of sins”) to both actions. This is exactly how the same phrase is used elsewhere:
Matthew 26:28 – Jesus’ blood was shed
eis aphesin hamartion
(“for the forgiveness of sins”) → clearly
in order to achieve
forgiveness, not because forgiveness had already occurred.
Mark 1:4 and Luke 3:3 – John’s baptism was
eis metanoian
(“for repentance”) → baptism led to / resulted in repentance.
Major Greek lexicons (BDAG, Thayer, Louw-Nida, etc.) list Acts 2:38 under the “purpose / in order to” category of
eis

, not under any causal (“because of”) meaning. In the 1st-century context, immediate baptism after repentance was the normal response to the gospel, showing that the two were tightly connected in the experience of conversion and forgiveness.
Sola Fide Understanding (the “because of / in view of” view)
Proponents of salvation by faith alone argue that
eis
can sometimes carry a
causal
or
reference
sense (“because of,” “on the basis of,” or “with reference to”). On this reading, Peter is saying: “Repent (and be baptized)
because of
the remission of sins” — i.e., baptism is the outward sign of an inward forgiveness that has already taken place through repentance and faith in Christ.
They support this with:
The ambiguity of the English word “for” (e.g., “Take aspirin
for
a headache” = because you have one).
Passages like Matthew 12:41 (“The men of Nineveh repented
eis
the preaching of Jonah” — often understood as “because of” Jonah’s preaching).
The immediate context: the crowd was already “cut to the heart” (v. 37), showing genuine conviction and repentance. Thus they are told to be baptized
because of
the forgiveness they have received by faith.
This view seeks to harmonize Acts 2:38 with the many clear “faith alone” passages (John 3:16, Acts 16:31, Romans 3–5, Ephesians 2:8-9, etc.).
Why we cannot use this verse as a conclusive proof text that
eis
MUST only mean “because of”
While the “because of” interpretation is possible and is sincerely held by many faithful Christians, it cannot be presented as the only or definitive meaning of
eis
in Acts 2:38 for these reasons:
Lexical evidence

overwhelmingly supports the “purpose” meaning (“in order to / unto”). No major Greek lexicon (BDAG, Thayer, etc.) lists “because of” as the meaning here; they consistently place it under purpose/result.
Even prominent Reformed Greek scholars who prefer the faith-alone position acknowledge the weakness of the causal view. Daniel Wallace notes that the linguistic evidence for a causal
eis
“fell short of proof.”
The exact phrase
eis aphesin hamartion
(“for the remission of sins”) appears in Matthew 26:28, where it clearly means Jesus’ blood was shed
in order to
forgive sins — not because sins were already forgiven. This parallel strongly favors the forward-looking “in order to” sense in Acts 2:38.
In summary:
Both interpretations are coherent and defended by godly scholars. The Greek allows some flexibility, but the most natural and lexically-supported reading of
eis
is
purpose

(“in order to / unto” remission of sins). At the same time, the verse is not an airtight proof text that forces us to reject the “because of” view. This is why sincere believers can disagree on this passage while still loving the Lord and one another.
Addition Context
The
main idea

of the passage is Peter's call for repentance and turning to Christ after the people recognized their role in Jesus' crucifixion. Peter includes both repentance and baptism as key steps in responding to the gospel message.
Cultural clues

: In the 1st century Jewish context, ritual washings were common as acts of purification. Baptism, in this case, symbolized a break from the past and a new identity in Christ. It was also closely associated with receiving the Holy Spirit, as the early church viewed these events as interconnected (Acts 2:41). Immediate baptism was the norm for new believers, emphasizing the seriousness of their commitment to follow Christ.
“And now why are you waiting? Arise and be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord.”
COC Understanding
: This verse explicitly ties baptism to the washing away of sins, indicating that baptism is necessary for sins to be forgiven.

The Church of Christ understands this verse as teaching that baptism is necessary for the washing away of sins. Ananias' instruction to Paul shows that, even after his conversion experience on the road to Damascus, Paul still needed to be baptized for his sins to be forgiven. Thus, baptism is seen as the moment when sins are cleansed.
Sola Fide Understanding
: "Washing away sins" is understood as a metaphor for spiritual cleansing, which is received by calling on the name of the Lord in faith. Baptism symbolizes this cleansing but does not cause it.

Supporters of sola fide interpret "wash away your sins" as metaphorical, with the actual cleansing of sin occurring when one "calls on the name of the Lord" in faith, as mentioned in Romans 10:13. Baptism is viewed as a symbolic act that represents the washing away of sins, but the true cleansing happens through faith in Christ’s work.
Additional Context
The
main idea

here is the urgency of Paul’s full conversion and participation in the Christian faith through baptism. Ananias encourages Paul to not delay but to complete his repentance by being baptized and identifying fully with Christ.
Cultural clues

: Paul’s audience would have been familiar with the idea of ritual cleansing. However, in the early Christian context, baptism was a decisive step marking one’s entrance into the community of believers and a public declaration of a break with sin. The language of "washing" reflects this cultural association with purification, which would have been understood both literally and symbolically by the early Jewish and Gentile converts.
5. Romans 6:3-4

“Or do you not know that as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? Therefore we were buried with Him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.”
COC Understanding
: Baptism is the means by which believers are united with Christ's death and resurrection, symbolizing the beginning of a new life, and is essential to salvation.

The Church of Christ sees baptism as the means by which believers are united with Christ’s death and resurrection. Baptism is more than symbolic; it is the moment when believers die to sin and are raised to new life in Christ. Without this identification with Christ’s death through baptism, salvation is incomplete.
Sola Fide Understanding
: Baptism is seen as a symbolic act representing the believer’s identification with Christ’s death and resurrection. Faith in Christ’s work is what saves, and baptism illustrates this truth.

Sola fide adherents understand this passage as describing the spiritual reality that occurs at conversion—when a believer, through faith, is united with Christ in His death and resurrection. Baptism is seen as the outward sign of this inward transformation, symbolizing the believer’s death to sin and new life in Christ. Salvation is secured by faith, not by the act of baptism.
Additional Context:
The
main idea

in Romans 6 is the believer's new identity in Christ. Paul emphasizes that just as Christ died and rose again, believers must die to sin and live a new life. Baptism symbolizes this transformation of a life genuinely changed for Christ.
Cultural clues

: Baptism in Paul’s time often involved full immersion in water, which symbolized burial and resurrection. This physical act powerfully conveyed the theological meaning of death to the old life and a resurrection to new life. In early Christian communities, this public act of baptism was a visible marker of one’s commitment to Christ.
6. Galatians 3:27
“For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.”
COC Understanding
: Baptism is the act through which a believer "puts on Christ," meaning it is necessary for entering into a relationship with Christ and receiving salvation.

The Church of Christ sees this verse as stating that baptism is the point at which one "puts on" Christ, meaning baptism is necessary for entering into a saving relationship with Christ and becoming part of the Christian community. Baptism is thus considered an essential act of obedience that results in salvation and unity with Christ.
Sola Fide Understanding
: Putting on Christ is viewed as a spiritual transformation that occurs through faith. Baptism is the outward expression of this reality, not the mechanism that initiates salvation.

From a faith-alone perspective, "putting on Christ" is understood as a spiritual transformation that happens through faith in Christ. Baptism is seen as the outward sign of this inward reality, symbolizing the believer’s union with Christ that comes through faith, but not the mechanism of salvation itself.
Additional Context
Main Idea of Galatians 3:
The overarching theme of this chapter is about
justification by faith in Jesus Christ, not by the works of the law.
Paul rebukes the Galatians for turning back to legalistic practices, insisting that faith in Christ brings righteousness, just as Abraham was justified by faith. Paul emphasizes that believers are
sons of God through faith
, and baptism serves as an expression of that faith and the believer’s new identity in Christ.
Cultural Clues:
In the 1st-century Greco-Roman world,
clothing was a powerful symbol

of status and identity. To "put on" Christ meant adopting a new identity as a member of the body of Christ. While baptism was the public ceremony signifying this change, the essential transformative act, according to Paul, was faith—being

"He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned."
COC Understanding

: This verse explicitly connects belief and baptism to salvation which suggests that both are essential. The absence of either results in not being saved. I also understand that the COC’s argument for the Sola Fide’s understanding is that, “if a person doesn’t even believe, don’t even need to talk about baptism”, which makes logical sense. But both understandings are still logically coherent.
Sola Fide Understanding
: The primary focus of this verse is on belief. The second part of the verse only mentions condemnation for unbelief, implying that faith, not baptism, is the critical factor in salvation.

Sola fide proponents argue that the emphasis of this verse is on belief, not baptism. They point out that the second half of the verse only condemns unbelief, without mentioning baptism, implying that faith is the key element for salvation. Baptism is understood as an important act of obedience, but not a requirement for salvation.
Additional context:
Main idea:

Mark 16 is the resurrection of Jesus and the commission to spread the Gospel. The chapter begins with the account of the women discovering the empty tomb, Jesus’ post-resurrection appearances, and ends with His commissioning of the disciples to go and preach the Gospel to all creation. It emphasizes the triumph of Jesus over death and the responsibility of His followers to proclaim this good news to the world. In verses
, Jesus gives the Great Commission, commanding His disciples to
“go into all the world and preach the gospel to all creation. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.”

Some biblical scholars hesitate to use Mark 16:9-20 (the "Longer Ending of Mark") as a proof text for doctrine due to significant concerns about its authenticity and textual history. I think due to these concerns, it is wise to utilise other parts of Scripture to form sound theological opinions.
1. Textual Evidence: Early Manuscripts Omit Mark 16:9-20

The most significant reason for caution is that the earliest and most reliable Greek manuscripts, including the Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus (4th century), do not contain Mark 16:9-20. Instead, these manuscripts end at Mark 16:8, with the women fleeing from the empty tomb in fear. This omission in two of the most respected early texts raises questions about whether these verses were part of the original Gospel of Mark.

Other early manuscripts include the shorter ending of Mark or other alternative endings, further showing that the longer ending was not universally accepted in the early church. These variations suggest that the longer ending was likely added later.
2. Style and Vocabulary Differences

Scholars who study the Greek text of Mark have observed that the style and vocabulary of Mark 16:9-20 differ from the rest of the Gospel. The Greek in this passage uses words and phrases that are not found elsewhere in Mark, and the overall tone feels different. This discrepancy suggests that a different author or editor may have added the longer ending at a later time, rather than it being the work of Mark himself.

For example, the repeated use of words like "Lord Jesus" (which is not common in Mark), and different phrasing patterns indicate a departure from Mark's usual narrative style. This shift creates uncertainty about its originality.
3. Patristic Evidence (Early Church Fathers)

The testimony of early Church Fathers also raises concerns about the inclusion of Mark 16:9-20. Eusebius of Caesarea (4th century) and Jerome (5th century) both noted that the longer ending of Mark was absent in many of the manuscripts they had access to. Eusebius, a prominent historian, even suggested that readers could end the Gospel at Mark 16:8 because the longer ending was not widely accepted.

While some early church leaders like Irenaeus (late 2nd century) seem to quote the longer ending, the testimony of Eusebius and Jerome indicates that the passage was not universally accepted or widely known among early Christian communities.
4. Theological Implications of Using the Longer Ending
Mark 16:9-20 includes several doctrines and practices, such as:
Baptism and salvation (Mark 16:16)
Handling snakes and drinking poison (Mark 16:18)
Signs and wonders (Mark 16:17-18)

Scholars are cautious about establishing doctrine based on a passage with textual uncertainty. Using Mark 16:16 to assert that baptism is necessary for salvation, for example, could be problematic because of the disputed authenticity of the passage. Similarly, the verses about handling snakes and drinking poison (which are not practiced by the broader Christian tradition) have historically led to dangerous misapplications in certain religious sects. Given the potential risks, scholars advise caution in deriving doctrines from these verses.
5. Scholars' Hypothesis: Why Was the Longer Ending Added?

Many scholars believe that the longer ending was likely added to provide a more satisfying conclusion to Mark's Gospel. Mark 16:8 ends abruptly, with the women fleeing the tomb in fear and saying nothing to anyone. This abrupt ending likely prompted early scribes or Christian communities to supplement the text with a more traditional resurrection appearance narrative, in line with the endings of the other Gospels (Matthew, Luke, and John). The longer ending includes post-resurrection appearances of Jesus, His commissioning of the disciples, and His ascension—elements more commonly found in the other Gospel accounts.

The longer ending likely emerged as an effort to harmonize Mark’s abrupt conclusion with the fuller resurrection stories found elsewhere in the New Testament. While this may explain why the longer ending was added, it also supports the argument that it may not have been part of the original Gospel of Mark.
Conclusion: Caution in Doctrine Formation

Due to the combination of textual omission in early manuscripts, differences in writing style, testimony from early Church Fathers, and the later addition theory, many biblical scholars advise caution in using Mark 16:9-20 as a definitive basis for forming doctrine. While the passage may reflect early Christian beliefs and practices, its disputed authenticity makes it less reliable as a foundation for key doctrinal teachings. Scholars prefer to rely on passages that are clearly supported by the earliest and most reliable manuscripts when formulating essential Christian doctrines.
8. John 3:5
Jesus answered, “Most assuredly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”
COC Understanding
: "Born of water" is understood as a reference to water baptism, making it essential for entering the kingdom of God.

The phrase "born of water and the Spirit" is interpreted as a direct reference to water baptism and the regenerating work of the Holy Spirit. For the church of Christ, this passage indicates that both elements—baptism in water and spiritual rebirth—are essential for salvation. Baptism is seen as the moment when a person is cleansed of sin and becomes part of the kingdom of God, in line with early Christian practices and other scriptures that link baptism with salvation.
Sola Fide Understanding
: The phrase "born of water and Spirit" is interpreted metaphorically, referring to spiritual rebirth by the Holy Spirit rather than a requirement for water baptism.

Advocates of sola fide view "born of water and the Spirit" as referring to two aspects of spiritual rebirth. The "water" is often interpreted symbolically, possibly referencing spiritual cleansing through the Word of God (as in
Ephesians 5:26

) or as a metaphor for purification. The emphasis is on the regenerating work of the Holy Spirit in the heart of the believer, which occurs through faith. According to this view, salvation comes through faith in Christ alone, and baptism is an important but secondary sign of the inner transformation brought about by the Spirit.
Additional Context
: Scholars debate whether "water" refers to literal water baptism or is symbolic of spiritual cleansing. Some see it as an allusion to Jewish purification rituals, while others view it in light of
Ezekiel 36:25-27

, where God promises to cleanse and give His Spirit. The broader biblical context emphasizes the role of faith in salvation, though baptism is closely linked with conversion and the reception of the Spirit in early Christian communities.
The
main idea

in John 3 is Jesus explaining the nature of spiritual rebirth to Nicodemus, indicating that entry into God's kingdom requires a transformation brought by the Spirit. Being "born again" points to a spiritual renewal rather than a simple physical or ritual action.
Cultural clues

: Nicodemus, a Pharisee, would have been familiar with ritual washings for purification, which may explain why Jesus used water imagery. However, Jesus extends the metaphor to include the Holy Spirit, pointing to a deeper, spiritual transformation. The language suggests a complete renewal, which, in the early Christian context, was associated with both the outward act of baptism and the inward work of the Spirit.

Strongest Argument for Church of Christ (COC) on Baptism
Argument:
The Church of Christ (COC) emphasizes that numerous New Testament verses explicitly link baptism to salvation. The clearest example comes from
Acts 2:38

, where Peter instructs the crowd, "Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit." This direct association of baptism with the "remission of sins" and receiving the Holy Spirit is seen as evidence that baptism is a necessary part of the salvation process. Additionally, verses like
Mark 16:16
("He who believes and is baptized will be saved") and
1 Peter 3:21

("There is also an antitype which now saves us—baptism") suggest that baptism plays an active role in salvation. COC proponents argue that the clear language in these verses shows that baptism is not merely symbolic but a necessary act of obedience and a means of grace for forgiveness and salvation.
Strongest Response Against It:
The strongest counterargument is that while baptism is commanded and important,
faith in Christ
is consistently presented as the sole requirement for salvation. In
John 3:16
, Jesus says, "whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life," without mentioning baptism. Similarly,
Ephesians 2:8-9
declares that "by grace you have been saved through faith... not of works," emphasizing that salvation comes through faith alone, apart from any additional actions, including baptism.
Romans 10:9

states that "if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you will be saved." The focus throughout the New Testament is on belief in Jesus as the core requirement for salvation, with baptism serving as an outward expression of that faith, not as a condition for salvation itself.
Acts 2:38
and similar verses can be interpreted as highlighting the importance of baptism, but they do not negate the foundational role of faith.
Strongest Argument for Sola Fide (Faith Alone)
Argument:
The doctrine of
sola fide

(faith alone) rests on the consistent teaching throughout Scripture that salvation comes solely through faith in Jesus Christ, without the need for additional works or rituals. The most direct evidence comes from
Ephesians 2:8-9

: "For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast." This passage clearly asserts that salvation is a gift of God, received by faith, and not dependent on human efforts or works, including baptism. Additionally,
Romans 3:28

declares, "Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith apart from the deeds of the law." The Apostle Paul consistently emphasizes that faith in Christ is sufficient for salvation, and that nothing we do, including being baptized, can add to the finished work of Christ on the cross. Baptism is seen as an important, obedient act that follows salvation, but it is not the means by which one is saved.
Strongest Response Against It:
The strongest argument against sola fide is that it risks underemphasizing the clear scriptural commands about baptism’s essential role in the salvation process. In
Acts 22:16

, Paul is instructed, "Arise and be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord." This verse directly links baptism with the washing away of sins, suggesting that baptism is more than just a symbolic act. Similarly,
1 Peter 3:21

states that "baptism... now saves us," which seems to indicate that baptism is an integral part of the salvation experience. While faith is unquestionably central, the New Testament presents baptism as a necessary response to that faith, and many passages connect the two in a way that cannot easily be dismissed. Proponents of the COC view argue that sola fide, by separating baptism from salvation, may overlook the full biblical teaching on the matter.

Some verses and points that led me to my current understanding:
1. Scriptural evidence
- Ephesians 2

“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God…” Saved through faith (which is a gift from God) rather than any particular action that we do to attain salvation.
- Galatians 3

Background of Galatians is that Gentile Christians fell into the trap of thinking they could earn salvation by “doing Jewish law things” but Paul reminds them that we are not justified by our actions but our faith in Jesus who died for us. Using this same principle, baptism should not be regarded as a final step in salvation, but rather, an outward declaration of our faith.
- Acts 2:38 vs Acts 3:19

Acts 2:38 is often used as the verse proving that baptism is necessary for salvation. The context of Acts 2 is that the apostles are preaching the gospel and tells the listeners to “be baptised for the remission of your sins”. In Acts 3, the apostles are also preaching the gospel, but this time, baptism is not mentioned at all. If baptism was indeed essential for salvation, he would’ve most definitely mentioned baptism to those whom he preached the gospel to. (I can send you some links on how Acts 2:38 is explained from the original Greek text after you digest this whole chunk!!)
- 1 Corinthians 1:14; 17

"I am thankful I did not baptise any of you..." Another verse that convinced me baptism is non-essential for salvation because if baptism was truly essential for salvation, an evangeliser like Paul would never have said he was thankful he did not baptise them (since his goal is to get as many people saved as possible!). Granted, the context was Paul speaking of divisiveness in the church, but my former point remains.
-1 Corinthians 1:17
Also, "for Christ did not send me to baptise, but to preach the gospel..."
2. Implications of believing of baptismal regeneration

Personally, the concept of baptismal regeneration led to my decision to get re-baptised at 15 years old (when I had originally gotten baptised at 12 because I feared not having the right understanding of baptism at the point in which I was baptised. In this case, we’ll never have the assurance of salvation because we can always worry about whether we “had the right understanding when we were baptised”, if we were “too young” or whether our entire body was submerged underwater during baptism. The verse “the truth will set you free” held new meaning for me when I realised baptism is not the ‘final step’ to salvation because I realised all my fears were for nothing - baptism has no power to save and my faith in Jesus’ death cleansing my sins had done it all. Baptism is simply an expression of my faith that I choose to do because I want to obey Him.

In summary, baptism is still very important. It cannot be disregarded or seen as not-important for a professing Christian. It’s a way to express our faith and obedience to Christ. But I don’t think it has any power to save us at all. We are already saved when we believe (not forgetting that true belief leads to repentance - so I doubt one’s belief if he claims to believe but does not repent).

When I was 16, I started thinking seriously: either Christianity is true and I’ll fully accept it, or if it’s false, I’m not going to waste any more Sundays. Looking back, I now see how God was drawing me to Him! In polytechnic, a debate assignment gave me the opportunity to discuss Creation vs Evolution. Naturally, I defended the Creation side since I grew up with a “Christian” background. That introduced me to apologetics, where I realized that believing in God is not merely blind faith; it can rest on solid logical evidence and arguments. Apologetics gave me my initial footing and showed me Christianity is logical and trustworthy.

At 17, I was ‘baptized’ and felt tremendous joy as I dedicated my life to Jesus! But the initial zeal slowly mellowed into a certain deadness in my faith. I understood that Jesus died for my sins, but I didn’t really grasp the depth of my sin. And without that, the price Jesus paid would remain superficial to me. So I prayed for God to help me understand the depth of my sin so I could truly appreciate the height of Jesus’s love.

That prayer was answered through a continuing struggle with lust and pornographic materials. Week after week, I promised to stop, only to fall again the next day. The endless cycle brought me to the deepest low I’ve ever experienced in my life, a feeling of utter despair and exhaustion. But as I kneeled down broken, it was there when His Word clicked: that Christ died for me not while I was perfect, but He died for me while I was a wretched sinner. And several years later, realizing that my righteous deeds are like filthy rags — it has always been purely by His grace alone.

Fast forward to Bukit Arang. Through patient teaching and loving conversations with the leaders here, God has deepened my understanding of the gospel. I now see even more clearly that salvation is not based on anything I do — not even good Christian acts or rituals — but
by grace alone, through faith alone, in Jesus alone
, ultimately
for God’s glory alone

So with that, I want to be baptized as the Bible presents it: a vivid picture of the dying, burial, and resurrection with Christ. I want to proclaim to the world that Jesus is historically and factually real. And the bad news is that we are dead in our sins because we chose to live by our own rules instead of our Creator’s design. But the good news is far greater — Christ has willingly paid our debt and ransomed us so we can be know and be known by God as we were created to be. To Him alone be the glory!
